Option C is incorrect — the Free Tier includes actual compute, storage, and other service usage, not just documentation. Option D confuses the Free Tier with support plan pricing. This combination lets students experiment with real GCP services without financial risk.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Always Free resources include: 1 e2-micro VM instance in select US regions, 5 GB of Cloud Storage (regional), 1 TB of BigQuery queries per month, 2 million Cloud Functions invocations per month, and several other service allowances that remain available indefinitely after the trial period.
  • The $300 free trial credits cannot be used for cryptocurrency mining or certain premium services, and GCP does not auto-charge when the trial expires — you must explicitly upgrade to a paid account to continue using services beyond Always Free limits.
  • After the 90-day trial, resources created with trial credits are stopped. You must upgrade to a paid account and restart them — this safety net prevents accidental charges for students and new users who forget about running resources.
  • Budget alerts are essential even on the Free Tier because exceeding Always Free limits on a paid account incurs charges. Setting a $0 or $1 budget alert on each project provides an early warning before unexpected costs accumulate.

questions.title: GCP Pricing Model
questions.scenario: A company wants to understand how they will be charged for running virtual machines in GCP.
questions.questionText: What pricing model does GCP primarily use for compute resources?

choices.text: Fixed monthly fee regardless of usage
Free for the first year, then charged annually
Pay-per-use with per-second billing for most compute resources

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GCP charges for compute resources based on actual usage measured in seconds, not fixed fees or annual contracts. You pay for exactly how long your VM runs, billed per second with a one-minute minimum.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GCP uses a pay-per-use model where you are charged based on actual resource consumption, with per-second billing for most compute services (minimum one-minute charge). Option B is wrong because GCP does not charge flat monthly fees for compute — costs vary with usage. Option C is incorrect because no upfront payment is required (though optional commitments offer discounts). Option D fabricates a pricing structure that does not exist. Stopping a VM stops compute charges immediately (persistent disk storage charges continue), giving you fine-grained cost control aligned with actual workload needs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Per-second billing applies to Compute Engine VMs, GKE node VMs, Dataproc clusters, Cloud SQL instances, and most other compute services — the one-minute minimum means a VM running for 90 seconds is billed for exactly 90 seconds, not rounded up to 2 minutes.
  • Storage is typically billed per GB-month, calculated by the average amount of data stored during the billing period. Persistent disks are charged whether the attached VM is running or stopped, which is a common source of unexpected costs.
  • Network egress (data leaving GCP to the internet or another region) is charged per GB, while ingress (data entering GCP) is generally free. Inter-zone traffic within a region incurs a small charge, and cross-region traffic costs more than intra-region traffic.
  • Pricing varies by region — US regions are generally cheapest, with European and Asian regions costing 5-20% more. Premium networking tier costs more than standard tier but provides lower latency through Google's private backbone network.

questions.title: Committed Use Discounts
questions.scenario: A company has predictable compute workloads running 24/7 and wants to reduce costs.
questions.questionText: What are Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) in GCP?

choices.text: Automatic discounts applied to all resources
Discounts for using resources only during off-peak hours
Discounts for committing to use specific resources for 1 or 3 years

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: CUDs provide significant discounts — up to 57% for 3-year terms — in exchange for committing to a minimum level of resource usage over a 1-year or 3-year period, regardless of whether you use the full committed amount.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) offer significant savings in exchange for committing to use specific amounts of compute resources for 1-year (up to 37% discount) or 3-year terms (up to 57% discount). Option A is wrong — CUDs require an explicit commitment and are not automatic (Sustained Use Discounts are automatic). Option C fabricates an off-peak pricing model that does not exist in GCP. Option D fabricates a deprecation discount that does not exist. CUDs are ideal for the scenario's predictable 24/7 workloads because the steady usage guarantees the committed resources will be fully utilized, maximizing savings.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GCP offers two types of CUDs: resource-based CUDs where you commit to specific amounts of vCPU and memory in a region (applied automatically to eligible VMs), and spend-based CUDs where you commit to a dollar amount of spending on specific services like Cloud SQL or Cloud Run.
  • Resource-based CUDs apply automatically to eligible usage in the committed region — you do not need to assign specific VMs to a commitment. If you commit to 16 vCPUs in us-central1, any combination of VMs using those vCPUs receives the discounted rate.
  • CUDs cannot be canceled once purchased — you are charged for the committed amount monthly for the entire term even if your actual usage drops below the commitment level. Careful capacity planning is essential before purchasing CUDs.
  • CUDs and Sustained Use Discounts do not stack — GCP applies the better discount. For workloads running 24/7, a 3-year CUD provides up to 57% savings compared to the 30% maximum from Sustained Use Discounts alone, making CUDs the better choice for predictable long-running workloads.

questions.title: Sustained Use Discounts
questions.scenario: A company runs Compute Engine instances continuously throughout the month without any special commitments.
questions.questionText: What are Sustained Use Discounts in GCP?

choices.text: Automatic discounts for resources running more than 25% of the month
Discounts for new GCP customers only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Sustained Use Discounts are automatic price reductions that kick in when you run Compute Engine resources for a significant portion of the month, increasing as usage increases — no commitment or action required from you.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs) are automatic discounts that GCP applies when Compute Engine resources run for a significant portion of the billing month. Discounts increase incrementally as usage grows, reaching up to 30% off for resources running the entire month. Option B describes Committed Use Discounts, which require an explicit commitment. Option C describes the discount model for Spot/Preemptible VMs, which is a separate mechanism. Option D is wrong — SUDs apply to all customers, not just new ones. The key advantage is that SUDs require no action, commitment, or configuration — they appear automatically on your bill.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SUDs are calculated in four incremental tiers based on monthly usage: 0-25% at full price, 25-50% at a reduced rate, 50-75% at a further reduced rate, and 75-100% at the lowest rate — the blended effective discount reaches approximately 30% for resources running all month.
  • GCP aggregates usage of the same machine type within a region across all VMs for SUD calculation — so running two n1-standard-4 VMs for half the month each is equivalent to running one for the full month, and both receive the combined sustained discount.
  • SUDs apply to vCPU and memory charges for N1, N2, and N2D general-purpose machine types, but notably do not apply to E2 machine types or to resources already covered by Committed Use Discounts — E2 instances are already priced lower as a cost-optimized family.
  • For workloads that run continuously, Committed Use Discounts provide larger savings than SUDs (up to 57% vs 30%), but SUDs serve as a no-commitment safety net for usage patterns that are not predictable enough to justify a commitment purchase.

questions.title: Preemptible and Spot VMs
questions.scenario: A company runs batch processing jobs that can tolerate interruptions and restart if needed.
questions.questionText: What is the benefit of using Spot VMs (formerly Preemptible VMs) in GCP?

choices.text: Up to 91% cost savings, but instances can be terminated with 30-second notice
Guaranteed uptime with premium support included
Free usage with no time limits

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Spot VMs use GCP's excess compute capacity at steep discounts of 60-91% off standard pricing, but the trade-off is that GCP can reclaim them at any time with only 30 seconds notice when capacity is needed for regular workloads.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Spot VMs offer 60-91% discounts compared to regular on-demand pricing by utilizing GCP's excess compute capacity. The trade-off is that GCP can terminate them with only 30 seconds notice when it needs the capacity back. Option B is the opposite of reality — Spot VMs have no uptime guarantee and no SLA. Option C is wrong because Spot VMs are not free, just heavily discounted. Option D is backwards — Spot VMs have lower scheduling priority than regular VMs. The scenario's fault-tolerant batch processing jobs are ideal because they can checkpoint progress and restart from where they left off after preemption.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Spot VMs replaced the older Preemptible VM model — the key difference is that Preemptible VMs had a hard 24-hour maximum runtime limit and were always terminated after 24 hours, while Spot VMs have no such time limit and run until preempted by capacity demands or stopped by the user.
  • Spot VMs have no SLA for availability and can be preempted at any time, making them unsuitable for user-facing production services, but perfect for batch processing, CI/CD pipelines, rendering jobs, scientific simulations, and any workload that can be interrupted and restarted.
  • Managed instance groups with Spot VMs automatically recreate instances after preemption, providing a self-healing compute pool — combined with checkpointing application state to Cloud Storage, this enables reliable batch processing at a fraction of on-demand cost.
  • You can mix Spot and regular VMs in the same managed instance group to balance cost savings with availability — for example, maintaining a baseline of regular VMs for steady work while adding Spot VMs for burst capacity during peak processing periods.

questions.title: GCP Pricing Calculator
questions.scenario: A company wants to estimate their monthly GCP costs before deploying resources.
questions.questionText: What tool can you use to estimate GCP costs before deploying resources?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Before deploying any resources, you can model your expected usage in GCP's web-based Pricing Calculator to generate estimated monthly costs and compare different configurations side by side.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The GCP Pricing Calculator is a free, web-based tool at cloud.google.com/products/calculator that lets you estimate costs by selecting GCP services, configuring specifications like machine types, storage amounts, and network usage, and viewing estimated monthly charges. Cloud Monitoring (option B) tracks performance metrics on already-running resources, not cost estimates. Cloud Debugger (option C) inspects running application code for bugs. Cloud Profiler (option D) analyzes application CPU and memory performance. None of these tools provide cost estimation — only the Pricing Calculator is designed for pre-deployment cost planning.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The Pricing Calculator at cloud.google.com/products/calculator supports all GCP services and lets you configure detailed specifications including machine type, region, storage class, network egress volume, and discount options (CUDs and SUDs) for accurate estimates.
  • Estimates can be saved, shared via URL with stakeholders, and exported for inclusion in budgeting documents and procurement processes — making it a collaborative planning tool, not just a personal calculator.
  • The calculator includes region-specific pricing, so you can compare cost differences between deploying in us-central1 versus asia-northeast1, which can be significant — some regions cost 20-40% more than the cheapest US regions for identical resources.
  • Calculator estimates are approximations based on the pricing at the time of estimation — actual costs may vary due to sustained use discounts, network usage patterns, dynamic pricing for some services, and any negotiated contract pricing that applies to your billing account.

questions.title: Budgets and Alerts
questions.scenario: A team wants to be notified when their GCP spending approaches a certain threshold to avoid unexpected charges.
questions.questionText: What GCP feature allows you to set spending thresholds and receive notifications?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GCP Budgets let you set a spending target for a billing account or project and configure alert thresholds — like 50%, 90%, and 100% — that trigger notifications when spending reaches those levels.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GCP Budgets allow you to set spending targets and configure alerts at percentage thresholds such as 50%, 90%, and 100% of the budget amount. Alerts notify stakeholders via email or Pub/Sub when spending approaches or exceeds the budget. Cloud Armor (option A) provides DDoS protection and web application firewall rules. Cloud Scheduler (option B) runs jobs on a cron schedule. VPC firewall rules (option C) control network traffic to and from VMs. None of these address cost management — only Budgets and budget alerts are designed to monitor spending and prevent cost surprises.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Budgets can be scoped to an entire billing account, specific projects, or filtered by labels and services — for example, creating a budget that only tracks Compute Engine spending in the production project, ignoring development costs.
  • Budget alerts are notifications only — they do not automatically stop spending or shut down resources. To automate cost control, connect budget alerts to Pub/Sub topics that trigger Cloud Functions to disable billing or stop resources programmatically.
  • Forecasted spend alerts use historical usage patterns to predict whether you will exceed the budget before the month ends, giving teams early warning even when current spending is below threshold — useful for catching gradual cost increases early.
  • Best practice is to create budgets at multiple levels: a billing-account-wide budget for total spending visibility, plus per-project budgets for granular control. Set alert thresholds at 50%, 80%, and 100% to provide multiple warning points before overspending occurs.

questions.title: Billing Export
questions.scenario: A finance team needs to analyze detailed GCP spending data in their business intelligence tools.
questions.questionText: How can you export detailed GCP billing data for analysis?

choices.text: View in Cloud Console without export option
Export billing data to BigQuery or Cloud Storage

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: GCP billing data can be exported to BigQuery for SQL-based analysis or to Cloud Storage as files. BigQuery export is the recommended approach because it enables detailed cost queries, custom dashboards, and integration with BI tools.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GCP allows exporting billing data to BigQuery for SQL-based analysis or to Cloud Storage as CSV/JSON files for external tool integration. Option A is misleading — PDF invoices exist but contain only summary data, not the detailed line-item records needed for analysis. Option B is wrong because billing exports are self-service and do not require support tickets. Option C is incorrect because the Console shows billing data but also provides export functionality. BigQuery export includes granular cost data with resource labels, SKU details, and usage amounts, enabling the finance team to build custom cost allocation reports and dashboards.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigQuery billing export includes three data tables: standard usage cost (line-item charges), detailed usage cost (resource-level charges with project and label attribution), and pricing data (the rate card applied to your account) — together providing complete cost transparency.
  • Once billing export is enabled, data flows automatically and historical data back to the export enablement date becomes available. There is no charge for storing billing data in the export dataset — Google covers the BigQuery storage cost for billing exports.
  • Looker Studio (formerly Data Studio) connects directly to BigQuery billing exports for visualization, and Google provides pre-built dashboard templates for common cost analysis views like spend-by-project, spend-by-service, and month-over-month trends.
  • Labels applied to GCP resources appear in billing export data, enabling cost allocation by any organizational dimension you define — team, environment, application, cost center — making consistent resource labeling essential for accurate financial reporting.

questions.title: Cloud SQL
questions.scenario: An application needs a managed relational database compatible with MySQL without managing database servers.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides fully managed relational databases for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The application needs a managed MySQL-compatible relational database without server management. Look for GCP's service that runs traditional relational database engines as a fully managed service with automated backups and patching.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud SQL is a fully managed relational database service supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. Google handles backups, replication, patches, encryption, and capacity management. Firestore (option A) is a NoSQL document database, not relational. Cloud Spanner (option B) is a globally distributed relational database designed for massive scale — far beyond what the scenario requires and significantly more expensive. Bigtable (option C) is a NoSQL wide-column database for high-throughput analytical workloads. Cloud SQL is the right choice for standard relational database needs with familiar MySQL compatibility and managed operations.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cloud SQL high-availability configuration creates a standby instance in a different zone with synchronous replication and automatic failover, providing a 99.95% SLA — the failover happens automatically with no application code changes required beyond connection retry logic.
  • Read replicas can be created in the same region or across regions to scale read operations and reduce latency for geographically distributed users — cross-region replicas also serve as disaster recovery targets for regional outages.
  • Private IP connectivity keeps database traffic within the VPC and off the public internet, improving both security and latency. Cloud SQL Auth Proxy provides secure, encrypted connections with IAM-based authentication for applications that need to connect from outside the VPC.
  • Automatic storage increase monitors disk usage and expands capacity before the database runs out of space, preventing out-of-disk outages that can corrupt data — the increase is transparent to applications with no downtime required.

questions.title: Virtual Private Cloud
questions.scenario: A company needs to create an isolated network environment for their GCP resources with control over IP addressing.
questions.questionText: What is a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) in GCP?

choices.text: A storage bucket with private access
A physical datacenter dedicated to one customer
A software-defined network providing connectivity for GCP resources

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: A VPC is a software-defined virtual network that provides isolated connectivity for your GCP resources. You control IP address ranges, subnets, routes, and firewall rules within it, similar to a traditional on-premises network but in the cloud.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: A VPC is a global, software-defined network that provides connectivity, isolation, and security for GCP resources like Compute Engine VMs, GKE clusters, and Cloud SQL instances. You define IP ranges, create subnets, configure routes, and set firewall rules. Option B confuses VPC with a dedicated physical datacenter, which would be Bare Metal Solution or a colocation arrangement. Option C confuses VPC with a VM, which is a compute resource that connects to a VPC. Option D confuses VPC with a Cloud Storage bucket, which is an object storage resource. VPCs are global in scope but contain regional subnets, providing a flexible networking layer that spans GCP's infrastructure.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• GCP VPCs are global resources, meaning a single VPC can contain subnets in different regions around the world — this is unique to GCP and different from AWS and Azure where virtual networks are regional, simplifying multi-region architectures.
  • Auto mode VPCs create one subnet per region automatically with predefined IP ranges, suitable for simple setups. Custom mode VPCs give you full control over subnet creation, IP addressing, and region selection — custom mode is recommended for production environments.
  • VPC peering connects two VPCs for private communication without going through the public internet, and Shared VPC allows a host project to share its VPC subnets with service projects — enabling centralized network management while letting teams deploy resources in their own projects.
  • Private Google Access allows VM instances without external IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, etc.) through internal routing, eliminating the need for NAT gateways or external IPs just to access GCP services.

questions.title: Cloud Monitoring
questions.scenario: An operations team needs to track the performance and health of their GCP resources and applications.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides metrics, dashboards, and alerting for monitoring resources?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Think about which aspect of system health the scenario is asking you to track and what kind of tool serves that purpose.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Monitoring (part of Google Cloud Operations Suite) collects metrics, events, and metadata from GCP resources and provides dashboards for visualization and alerting policies for automated notifications. Cloud Debugger (option B) was a tool for inspecting application code state in production (now deprecated). Cloud Build (option C) is a CI/CD service for building and testing code. Cloud Deploy (option D) is a managed delivery service for deploying to GKE and Cloud Run. Only Cloud Monitoring provides the metrics, dashboards, and alerting combination that operations teams need for resource health tracking.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cloud Monitoring integrates with Cloud Logging to provide unified observability — metrics show you what is happening quantitatively, while logs explain why. Together they form the core of GCP's Operations Suite for troubleshooting and performance optimization.
  • Custom metrics can be created for application-specific data using the Monitoring API or OpenTelemetry, enabling you to track business KPIs alongside infrastructure metrics on the same dashboards and alerting policies.
  • Uptime checks probe external HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP endpoints from multiple global locations at configurable intervals, alerting you when your services become unreachable — providing external-perspective monitoring that catches issues invisible from inside the network.
  • Alert policies can notify through multiple channels including email, SMS, Slack, PagerDuty, OpsGenie, and custom webhooks, and can be configured with conditions like metric thresholds, absence of data, or forecasted values — enabling proactive incident response before users are affected.

questions.title: Cloud Logging
questions.scenario: A security team needs to collect and analyze logs from all GCP resources for compliance and troubleshooting.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides centralized log management and analysis?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider what the operations team needs to collect and where they need to analyze it to meet the scenario's requirements.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Logging (part of Google Cloud Operations Suite) is a fully managed service for storing, searching, analyzing, and alerting on log data from GCP resources and custom applications. Cloud Trace (option B) collects distributed tracing data for analyzing request latency across microservices. Cloud Profiler (option C) continuously analyzes CPU and memory usage of production applications. Cloud Scheduler (option D) triggers jobs on a cron schedule and has nothing to do with log management. Cloud Logging automatically ingests admin activity logs, data access logs, and system event logs from GCP services, providing the centralized compliance view the security team needs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The Log Router is the core of Cloud Logging's architecture — it evaluates every log entry against configured sinks to determine where logs are stored. Sinks can direct logs to Cloud Logging buckets for searching, BigQuery for analytics, Cloud Storage for archival, or Pub/Sub for streaming to external SIEM tools.
  • Log-based metrics convert specific log patterns into Cloud Monitoring metrics, enabling dashboards and alerts based on log content — for example, creating a metric that counts HTTP 500 errors in application logs and alerting when the rate exceeds a threshold.
  • Cloud Audit Logs are a critical subset of Cloud Logging for security teams: Admin Activity logs (always on, free, 400-day retention) track configuration changes, while Data Access logs (must be enabled, charged for ingestion) track reads and writes to user data for compliance auditing.
  • Default log retention in Cloud Logging is 30 days for most log types and 400 days for Admin Activity logs. Custom retention periods can be configured per log bucket, and routing logs to Cloud Storage or BigQuery provides unlimited long-term retention for compliance requirements that exceed default periods.

questions.title: Organization Policies
questions.scenario: A security administrator wants to enforce that no one can create resources outside of approved regions.
questions.questionText: What GCP feature allows administrators to set constraints on resource configurations across the organization?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Consider the specific requirements and constraints in the scenario to determine which option best addresses all of them.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Organization Policy Service allows administrators to set constraints that control how resources can be configured across the organization. Unlike IAM, which controls who can perform actions, organization policies control what configurations are allowed. IAM roles (option B) grant permissions to identities but cannot restrict resource locations. VPC firewall rules (option C) control network traffic, not resource configurations. Cloud Armor (option D) provides DDoS protection and WAF capabilities. The scenario's requirement to restrict resource creation to approved regions is exactly what the gcp.resourceLocations organization policy constraint enforces.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Organization policy constraints can allow, deny, or enforce specific configurations — the gcp.resourceLocations constraint restricts which regions and zones resources can be created in, while iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation blocks key file generation across the organization.
  • Policies inherit down the resource hierarchy and can be overridden at lower levels if the parent policy allows it — for example, setting a restrictive region policy at the Organization level but exempting a specific folder for a team that legitimately needs resources in additional regions.
  • Common constraints include: gcp.resourceLocations (restrict regions), compute.vmExternalIpAccess (deny public IPs on VMs), iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains (restrict IAM grants to specific domains), and storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess (require uniform access on all buckets).
  • Custom organization policy constraints allow you to define organization-specific rules beyond Google's predefined constraints — for example, requiring all Cloud SQL instances to use private IP only, or mandating that all Compute Engine VMs use a specific minimum machine type.

questions.title: Disaster Recovery
questions.scenario: A company needs to ensure their critical applications can recover quickly if an entire region becomes unavailable.
questions.questionText: What is the best approach for disaster recovery across GCP regions?

choices.text: Rely on single-region deployment with extra VMs
Disable automatic updates to prevent failures
Use only local backups on the same disk
Deploy resources in multiple regions with data replication and failover mechanisms

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Regional disasters require resources running in geographically separate regions with data replicated between them. Extra VMs in the same region do not protect against a full regional outage; only multi-region architecture provides that resilience.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Disaster recovery for regional failures requires deploying resources across multiple GCP regions with data replication and failover mechanisms. Option B fails because extra VMs in the same region all go down during a regional outage. Option C fails because local backups on the same disk are lost if the disk or zone fails. Option D is counterproductive — disabling updates does not prevent infrastructure failures and leaves systems vulnerable to known bugs. GCP provides multi-region Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL cross-region replicas, and global HTTP(S) load balancing that automatically routes traffic away from failed regions to healthy ones.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines how quickly the system must recover, and RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines how much data loss is acceptable — these two metrics drive architecture decisions: lower RTO/RPO requires more infrastructure investment in replication and standby systems.
  • GCP supports multiple DR patterns: hot standby (full replica running in another region, near-zero RTO/RPO but highest cost), warm standby (scaled-down replica that can be scaled up during failover), and cold standby (infrastructure-as-code templates that deploy a new environment from backups when needed, lowest cost but highest RTO).
  • Multi-region Cloud Storage classes (dual-region and multi-region) automatically replicate data across regions with strong consistency, providing built-in geographic redundancy for object data without manual replication configuration.
  • Global HTTP(S) Load Balancing distributes traffic across backend services in multiple regions and automatically routes around regional failures using health checks — when backends in one region become unhealthy, traffic shifts to healthy backends in other regions within seconds, enabling near-instant failover for stateless web applications.

questions.title: GCP Support Plans
questions.scenario: A company is evaluating GCP and wants to understand what support options are available.
questions.questionText: What support options does Google Cloud provide?

choices.text: Free basic support, plus paid tiers (Standard, Enhanced, Premium) with faster response times
Only premium paid support with 24/7 phone access
Community forums only with no official support
Support is included free for all customers at all levels

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Google Cloud provides a tiered support model starting with free Basic support for all customers, plus three paid tiers — Standard, Enhanced, and Premium — each offering progressively faster response times and more proactive assistance.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: GCP provides multiple support tiers: Basic (free, self-service documentation and community forums), Standard (paid, business-hours technical support), Enhanced (paid, 24/7 support for critical issues with faster response times), and Premium (paid, fastest response with a dedicated Technical Account Manager). Option A is wrong because free Basic support exists for all customers. Option B is incorrect because advanced support features require paid plans. Option C understates the offering — even Basic support includes billing support and documentation, not just forums. Higher tiers offer faster response times, proactive guidance, and dedicated resources for organizations with mission-critical workloads.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Basic support provides self-service documentation, community forums on Google Cloud Community, and billing-only support cases — it is suitable for development environments and non-critical workloads where teams can troubleshoot independently.
  • Standard support offers unlimited technical support cases during business hours with a 4-hour initial response time for high-impact (P2) issues, making it appropriate for organizations running production workloads that need professional troubleshooting assistance.
  • Enhanced support provides 1-hour response for critical (P1) issues with 24/7 coverage, proactive technical guidance, and access to Cloud Support API for programmatic case management — designed for organizations where production downtime has significant business impact.
  • Premium support delivers 15-minute response for P1 issues, a dedicated Technical Account Manager (TAM) who understands your architecture, proactive health reviews, training credits, and event management support — the highest tier for enterprises where cloud availability directly impacts revenue.

gl-cloud-computing.name: Cloud Computing
gl-cloud-computing.definition: The on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing, eliminating the need to own and maintain physical datacenters and servers.
gl-cloud-computing.examNote: NIST defines 5 characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service.

gl-iaas.name: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
gl-iaas.definition: Cloud service model providing virtualized computing resources where the customer manages OS, middleware, runtime, and applications.
gl-iaas.examNote: Compute Engine is GCP's primary IaaS offering. Maximum control, maximum responsibility.

gl-paas.name: Platform as a Service (PaaS)
gl-paas.definition: Cloud service model providing a platform for developing and deploying applications without managing underlying infrastructure.
gl-paas.examNote: App Engine and Cloud Run are GCP PaaS offerings. Focus on code, not infrastructure.

gl-saas.name: Software as a Service (SaaS)
gl-saas.definition: Cloud service model delivering complete software applications over the internet, accessed through web browsers without installation.
gl-saas.examNote: Google Workspace (Gmail, Docs, Drive) is Google's SaaS offering. Minimal customer responsibility.

gl-region.name: Region
gl-region.definition: A specific geographic location containing multiple zones where GCP resources can be deployed.
gl-region.examNote: Regions are independent; choose based on latency, compliance, and service availability. Examples: us-central1, europe-west1.

gl-zone.name: Zone
gl-zone.definition: An isolated deployment area within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking infrastructure.
gl-zone.examNote: Deploy across multiple zones for high availability. Zone format: region-zone (e.g., us-central1-a).

gl-project.name: Project
gl-project.definition: The base-level organizing entity in GCP that contains resources, manages billing, and controls access.
gl-project.examNote: Every resource belongs to exactly one project. Project ID is globally unique and immutable.

gl-organization.name: Organization
gl-organization.definition: The root node of the GCP resource hierarchy, representing a company and providing centralized visibility and control.
gl-organization.examNote: Requires Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain. Enables organization policies and centralized IAM.

gl-folder.name: Folder
gl-folder.definition: An optional grouping mechanism in the resource hierarchy for organizing projects by team, department, or environment.
gl-folder.examNote: IAM and organization policies set at folder level inherit to all contained projects.

gl-iam.name: Identity and Access Management (IAM)
gl-iam.definition: GCP's system for controlling who (identity) can do what (permissions) on which resources (scope).
gl-iam.examNote: Policies are additive with no explicit deny. Use predefined roles over basic roles for least privilege.

gl-role.name: IAM Role
gl-role.definition: A collection of permissions that can be granted to principals (users, groups, service accounts) at a scope.

gl-service-account.name: Service Account
gl-service-account.definition: A special account used by applications and services (not humans) to authenticate and access GCP resources.
gl-service-account.examNote: Avoid key files; use attached service accounts. Default service accounts have broad permissions.

gl-billing-account.name: Billing Account
gl-billing-account.definition: A payment entity linked to one or more projects that defines who pays for GCP resource usage.
gl-billing-account.examNote: Projects need a billing account to use paid services. One billing account can link to many projects.

gl-compute-engine.name: Compute Engine
gl-compute-engine.definition: GCP's IaaS service providing virtual machines with customizable configurations running on Google infrastructure.
gl-compute-engine.examNote: Offers preemptible/spot VMs for cost savings, custom machine types, and live migration during maintenance.

gl-app-engine.name: App Engine
gl-app-engine.definition: GCP's fully managed PaaS for building and deploying web applications without managing infrastructure.
gl-app-engine.examNote: Two environments: Standard (sandbox, fast scaling) and Flexible (container-based). Supports multiple languages.

gl-cloud-storage.name: Cloud Storage
gl-cloud-storage.definition: GCP's unified object storage service for storing and accessing unstructured data like files, images, and backups.
gl-cloud-storage.examNote: Four storage classes: Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive. Objects stored in buckets.

gl-bigquery.name: BigQuery
gl-bigquery.definition: GCP's serverless, highly scalable data warehouse for running SQL queries on massive datasets.
gl-bigquery.examNote: Separates storage and compute. Supports streaming and batch. Includes BigQuery ML for machine learning.

gl-vpc.name: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
gl-vpc.definition: A global, software-defined network providing connectivity, isolation, and security for GCP resources.
gl-vpc.examNote: VPCs are global; subnets are regional. Auto mode creates subnets automatically; custom mode for full control.

gl-gke.name: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
gl-gke.definition: GCP's managed Kubernetes service for deploying, managing, and scaling containerized applications.
gl-gke.examNote: Autopilot mode fully manages nodes; Standard mode offers more control. Integrated with Google Cloud services.

gl-cloud-functions.name: Cloud Functions
gl-cloud-functions.definition: GCP's serverless, event-driven compute service for running code in response to events without managing servers.
gl-cloud-functions.examNote: Pay only for execution time. Triggered by HTTP, Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage events. 2nd gen built on Cloud Run.
